newsitem.title: USA: Ribi expands deal with SmithKline Beecham.
newsitem.headline: Ribi expands deal with SmithKline Beecham.

text.p: Ribi ImmunoChem Research Inc said Tuesday it made an agreement expanding the right of SmithKline Beecham Biologicals (SB Bio), the vaccine development subsidiary of SmithKline Beecham, to use Ribi adjuvants in its vaccines under development.
The company said it will provide Ribi with added cash flow in the form of license fees, supply payments and royalties upon commercialization as well as equity over three years.

Under this most recent agreement, Ribi has granted SB Bio an exclusive license to use Ribi adjuvants commercially in a human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, a co-exclusive license for a tuberculosis vaccine and a non-exclusive license to use Ribi adjuvants in the development of additional infectious disease as well as other vaccines. In addition to annual license fees, Ribi will receive transfer payments for clinical and commercial quantities of adjuvant and royalties on any commercial sales of approved HPV, tuberculosis or other vaccines incorporating its adjuvants.

HPV (human papillomavirus) is a sexually transmitted disease that causes genital warts, which can lead to cervical cancer. It has been estimated that genital wart infections in the U.S. increased at twice the rate of genital herpes infections, another serious sexually transmitted disease, over the last 10 years. An estimated 1 million new cases of genital warts are diagnosed in the U.S. each year and an estimated 40 million persons in the U.S. are infected with genital warts. An estimated 500,000 new cases of cervical cancer occur each year worldwide, with 80 percent of the cases occurring in developing countries. Cervical cancer is the second most frequent tumor in women on a worldwide basis with HPV found in more than 90 percent of cervical cancer patients.

Tuberculosis, which can lay dormant for extended periods, has re-emerged as a serious disease threat because of new strains that have developed resistance to multiple antibiotics, putting at risk not only infected persons but others who may have close contact with infected persons.
